section.title: The Book of Consolation
section.sectionRationale: In the middle of a book dominated by judgment, Jeremiah is told to write down a sustained oracle of pure hope: Jacob's distress will end in salvation, the broken nation will be rebuilt, mourning will turn to joy, and, at the very center of it all, God will make a new covenant, writing His law on hearts rather than tablets and forgiving sin once for all.
section.thesis: God's discipline of His people through exile is real and just, but it is not His last word, His unbreakable love guarantees a future restoration that culminates in a new covenant of inward transformation and full forgiveness, the very covenant Christ inaugurates at the Last Supper and the cross.
section.frameNote: Eight scenes: restoration promised amid the day of Jacob's trouble; an incurable wound that God alone heals; the city rebuilt under a ruler from their own midst; everlasting love rebuilding Virgin Israel; Rachel's weeping turned to hope; the land resettled and personal responsibility restored; the new covenant of the heart, the summit of the whole book; and God's covenant faithfulness as fixed as creation itself, sealed in a holy, rebuilt Jerusalem.

units.label: Restoration and the day of Jacob's trouble

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD:
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you.

For behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah, declares the LORD. I will restore them to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they will possess it.’”
These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah.

Yes, this is what the LORD says: 
“A cry of panic is heard, a cry of terror, not of peace.

Ask now, and see: Can a male give birth? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor 
and every face turned pale?
How awful that day will be! None will be like it! It is the time of Jacob's distress, but he will be saved out of it.

On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will break the {{ol|yoke}} off their necks and tear off their bonds, 
and no longer will strangers enslave them.

Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, 
whom I will raise up for them.

As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, declares the LORD, and do not be dismayed, O Israel. For I will surely save you out of a distant place, your descendants from the land of their captivity! Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid.

For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD. Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you. Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.”

units.label: An incurable wound, a faithful healer
units.note: who no one cares for, He does

verses.text:
For this is what the LORD says: 
“Your injury is incurable; your wound is grievous.

There is no one to plead your cause, no remedy for your sores, 
no recovery for you.
All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you, for I have struck you as an enemy would, with the discipline of someone cruel, because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins.

Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain has no cure! Because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins 
I have done these things to you.

Nevertheless, all who devour you will be devoured, and all your adversaries, every one of them, will go off into exile. Those who plundered you will be plundered, and all who raided you will be raided.
But I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD, because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares.”

units.label: The city rebuilt, a ruler from their own midst

verses.text:
This is what the LORD says: 
“I will restore the fortunes of Jacob's tents and have compassion on his dwellings. And the city will be rebuilt on her own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place.
Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration. I will multiply them, and they will not be decreased; I will honor them, and they will not be belittled.

Their children will be as in days of old, and their congregation will be established before Me; 
and I will punish all their oppressors.

Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst. And I will bring him near, and he will approach Me, for who would dare on his own to approach Me?” declares the LORD.
“And you will be My people, and I will be your God.”
Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked.
The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart. In the days to come you will understand this.
“At that time,” declares the LORD, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be My people.”

This is what the LORD says: 
“The people who survived the sword found favor in the wilderness 
when Israel went to find rest.”

The LORD appeared to us in the past, saying: 
“I have loved you with an {{ahavatOlam|everlasting love}}; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion.
Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel. Again you will take up your tambourines and go out in joyful dancing.
Again you will plant vineyards on the hills of Samaria; the farmers will plant and enjoy the fruit.
For there will be a day when watchmen will call out on the hills of Ephraim, ‘Arise, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God!’”

For this is what the LORD says: 
“Sing with joy for Jacob; shout for the foremost of the nations! Make your praises heard, and say, ‘O LORD, save Your people, 
the remnant of Israel!’

Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, including the blind and the lame, expectant mothers and women in labor. 
They will return as a great assembly!

They will come with weeping, and by their supplication I will lead them; I will make them walk beside streams of waters, on a level path where they will not stumble. For I am Israel's Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn.”

Hear, O nations, the word of the LORD, and proclaim it in distant coastlands: 
“The One who scattered Israel will gather them and keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock.
For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and redeemed him from the hand that had overpowered him.

They will come and shout for joy on the heights of Zion; they will be radiant over the bounty of the LORD, the grain, new wine, and oil, and the young of the flocks and herds. Their life will be like a well-watered garden, and never again will they languish.
Then the maidens will rejoice with dancing, young men and old as well. I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow.
I will fill the souls of the priests abundantly, and will fill My people with My goodness,” declares the LORD.

This is what the LORD says: 
“A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, 
because they are no more.”

This is what the LORD says: 
“Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for the reward for your work will come, declares the LORD. Then your children will return from the land of the enemy.
So there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children will return to their own land.

I have surely heard Ephraim's moaning: 
‘You disciplined me severely, like an untrained calf. Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God.
After I returned, I repented; and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh in grief. I was ashamed and humiliated because I bore the disgrace of my youth.’

Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child? Though I often speak against him, I still remember him. Therefore My heart yearns for him; I have great compassion for him,” declares the LORD.
“Set up the roadmarks, establish the signposts. Keep the highway in mind, the road you have traveled. Return, O Virgin Israel, return to these cities of yours.
How long will you wander, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing in the land, a woman will shelter a man.”

units.label: The land resettled, sour grapes no more
units.note: each will die for his own iniquity

verses.text: This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “When I restore them from captivity, they will once again speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities: ‘May the LORD bless you, O righteous dwelling place, O holy mountain.’
And Judah and all its cities will dwell together in the land, the farmers and those who move with the flocks,
for I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak.”
At this I awoke and looked around. My sleep had been most pleasant to me.
“The days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and of beast.
Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down, to demolish, destroy, and bring disaster, so I will watch over them to build and to plant,” declares the LORD.

“In those days, it will no longer be said: 
‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge.’
Instead, each will die for his own iniquity. If anyone eats the sour grapes, his own teeth will be set on edge.

units.label: The new covenant
units.note: My law within them, written on their hearts

verses.text: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a {{beritChadashah|new covenant}} with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.

It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD.

“But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.

No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all {{yada|know}} Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”

units.label: Fixed as creation, a holy city rebuilt

verses.text: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day, who sets in order the moon and stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar, the LORD of Hosts is His name:
“Only if this fixed order departed from My presence, declares the LORD, would Israel's descendants ever cease to be a nation before Me.”

This is what the LORD says: 
“Only if the heavens above could be measured and the foundations of the earth below searched out would I reject all of Israel's descendants because of all they have done,” declares the LORD.
“The days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when this city will be rebuilt for Me, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate.
The measuring line will once again stretch out straight to the hill of Gareb and then turn toward Goah.

The whole valley of the dead bodies and ashes, and all the fields as far as the Kidron Valley, to the corner of the Horse Gate to the east, will be holy to the LORD. It will never again be uprooted or demolished.”

ol.gloss: A yoke, the wooden crossbar of imposed servitude. Judah had been told to wear Babylon's yoke as God's appointed discipline, Jeremiah 27 to 28; here God promises the day is coming when He Himself will break that yoke off His people's necks.

ahavatOlam.gloss: Everlasting love, love without end. God grounds the whole restoration not in Israel's worthiness but in a love that reaches back before their sin and forward past their exile, the reason He keeps drawing His people back to Himself.

beritChadashah.gloss: New covenant. Unlike the Sinai covenant, external and broken, this covenant places God's law within His people and forgives their sin completely; the New Testament identifies this as the covenant Christ inaugurates in His blood, Luke 22:20, Hebrews 8:8-12.

yada.gloss: To know, intimately and experientially, not merely intellectually. Under the new covenant every one of God's people will yada Him directly, from the least to the greatest, no longer dependent on another to teach them who He is.

basic.context: In the middle of oracles of judgment, Jeremiah is commanded to write down an entire book of consolation. Jacob's coming distress will end in salvation, the incurable wound will be healed, the ruined city rebuilt, Rachel's weeping turned to joy, and, at the center of it all, God promises a new covenant unlike the one broken at Sinai: His law written on hearts, not tablets, and sins remembered no more.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, future restoration for God's exiled people, one whose language of gathering, rebuilding, and covenant renewal the New Testament explicitly takes up. The new covenant of 31:31-34 is not a vague spiritual metaphor; Jesus quotes its very language over the cup at the Last Supper, Luke 22:20, and Hebrews quotes the whole passage to explain the difference Christ's blood makes.
basic.originalLanguages: God's restoration flows from an ahavat olam, an everlasting love, that predates and outlasts Israel's unfaithfulness. It climaxes in a berit chadashah, a new covenant, in which God's people will yada Him, know Him directly and intimately, rather than depending on another to teach them, because their sins are forgiven and remembered no more.
basic.typology: The broken yoke anticipates the true freedom Christ offers, Matthew 11:29-30. The healing of an incurable wound anticipates the atonement that heals what nothing else could, 1 Peter 2:24. Above all, the new covenant of the heart anticipates and is directly named as fulfilled in Christ's blood, poured out for many, Luke 22:20, Hebrews 8:8-12.
basic.christ: Jeremiah 31:31-34 is the Old Testament's clearest promise of the new covenant, and the New Testament repeatedly identifies Jesus as the one who establishes it. At the Last Supper He takes the cup and says, this cup is the new covenant in My blood, Luke 22:20, deliberately using Jeremiah's own words. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes this passage at length to show that Christ's priesthood and sacrifice have made the first covenant obsolete.
basic.god: God disciplines His people justly for real sin, yet His anger is not His last word; His everlasting love guarantees He will heal, rebuild, and forgive completely. He is as reliable in His covenant faithfulness as the fixed order of the sun, moon, and sea, so certain that only the undoing of creation itself could undo His promise to His people.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 22:20 records Jesus naming the cup of the Last Supper as the new covenant in My blood, directly invoking this passage. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full to explain Christ's superior priesthood. Matthew 2:17-18 applies Rachel's weeping in 31:15 to the slaughter of the infants at Bethlehem. Matthew 11:28-30 answers the broken yoke of 30:8 with Christ's own easy yoke.
basic.oneStory: The Book of Consolation promises that God's discipline of His exiled people will not be His last word: He will heal, rebuild, and gather them, and above all make a new covenant that changes hearts and forgives sin completely. That covenant is not a future hope deferred forever; the New Testament shows Jesus establishing it in His own blood, so that everyone who trusts Him already lives under the new covenant Jeremiah foresaw.

context.literary:
Chapters 30 and 31 are a block of poetry in a book that is mostly prose and judgment, and the block has its own title and its own end. It opens with a command to write, 30:2, and it closes with a vision of a holy city that will never again be uprooted, 31:38 to 40. In between, the oracles run in a pattern of alternation between fear and rescue: the cry of terror in 30:5 to 7 gives way to salvation, the incurable wound of 30:12 to 15 to healing in 30:17, the ruins of 30:18 to the rebuilt city, Rachel's weeping in 31:15 to the promise in 31:16 to 17. Each time the grief is stated fully and then answered.

The poems also run on the repetition of one root, shuv, to turn or return. It appears again and again from 31:8 to 31:22: the exiles return, Rachel's children return, Ephraim asks to be 'restored that I may return,' and the 'faithless daughter' is, in the Hebrew, the 'turning' daughter. The language of coming home is the language of repentance, and the passage does not separate the two.

The new covenant of 31:31 to 34 is set within the block as its summit. It follows the verses on personal responsibility, 31:29 to 30, and it is followed by the oath of the fixed order of creation, 31:35 to 37. Notice the one narrative interruption in 31:26: 'At this I awoke and looked around. My sleep had been most pleasant to me.' The prophet tells us that these oracles reached him as something like a dream of comfort, a rare gentle moment in a book of tears. The note also reminds us that Jeremiah, who had been told to uproot and tear down, was here allowed to see what he was to build and plant.
context.historical:
The oracles most likely belong to the years after 597, when the first deportation had fallen on Judah, and before the fall of Jerusalem in 586. They are addressed to 'Israel and Judah,' 30:3, and the poetry reaches back to the northern kingdom, whose people had been carried off by Assyria in 722 BC. Ephraim, Samaria and Rachel in 31:4 to 20 are names from the north, and Ramah, where Rachel weeps, is a town north of Jerusalem in Benjamin. Jeremiah himself would later be released there from the chains of the captives, Jeremiah 40:1, which makes the town a staging place for exiles. Rachel was the mother of Joseph, from whom Ephraim descended, and of Benjamin. Her tomb was tied to this region, Genesis 35:19 and 1 Samuel 10:2, so her weeping at Ramah speaks for the mothers of both north and south.

The promise of return was not a fantasy for the people who first heard it. The northern tribes had been scattered for over a century, and southern Judah's hope was equally precarious. In this setting 'the days are coming' was a daring thing to say, and 'write in a book,' 30:2, makes it a pledge against the day it would be needed. Jeremiah 36 shows that books were exactly what Jehoiakim tried to destroy, and the command to write is an assurance that the promise cannot be burned.

The chapter 31 city, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate, 31:38, names real landmarks on Jerusalem's north and west sides, as does the line to Gareb and Goah. The vow that the whole valley of 'dead bodies and ashes' will be holy to the LORD, 31:40, takes the places of Jerusalem's worst memories, the valleys of death and defilement, and consecrates them. The people who first heard it knew what ruin meant, and they were being promised a city holier than the one that fell.
context.canonical:
The new covenant of 31:31 to 34 is the only place in the Old Testament that uses the phrase, and the New Testament reads it as the key to its own self-understanding. Jesus names the cup the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant, 'not of the letter but of the Spirit,' 2 Corinthians 3:6. Hebrews 8:8 to 12 quotes the whole of Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, comments on it in 8:13, and cites its closing lines again in Hebrews 10:15 to 18 to argue that where sins are forgiven, no more offering for sin is needed. Hebrews 12:24 calls Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.

The promise itself is a point where several streams meet. The promise to write the law on the heart is paralleled in Ezekiel 36:26 to 27, with its heart of flesh and the gift of the Spirit, and in Deuteronomy 30:6, which speaks of God circumcising the heart. The promise of a Davidic king, 30:9, belongs with Jeremiah 23:5 to 6 and 33:15 to 16, with Ezekiel 34:23 and with Hosea 3:5. The proverb about sour grapes in 31:29 is taken up and answered in Ezekiel 18:2 to 4. The weeping of Rachel in 31:15 is applied by Matthew to the killing of the infants at Bethlehem, Matthew 2:17 to 18.

The oath of the fixed order in 31:35 to 37 is repeated in 33:20 to 21, and the everlasting love of 31:3 meets Isaiah 54:10, 'My loving devotion will not depart from you.' Lamentations 3:22 to 23, written in the ruins, confesses the same faithfulness. The 'everlasting covenant' of 32:40 and 50:5 is the same covenant by another name.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah wanted a people crushed by judgment to know that judgment was neither the whole story nor a sign of God's rejection. The block is designed to be read in exile, as a book to be kept and opened when the nation could no longer trust its eyes. It insists that the wound is real and deserved, 30:14 to 15, and that the cure is no less real. It does not ask the people to pretend that the pain is small, only to believe that God is greater.

He also wanted to correct a wrong reading of the exile. The people had a proverb that said the children were paying for the fathers' sins, 31:29. The promise is that each generation will be responsible before God for its own life, and the new covenant answers the underlying problem: the old covenant was broken, 31:32, and the cure is not a better effort by the same people but a different kind of covenant, with a law written within. The first hearers were meant to understand that their hope rested on what God would do in them, not on what they could do for Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These chapters describe what God promises to do. They do not command the reader to produce the restoration or to bring in the new covenant by effort. The imperatives that do appear, 'keep your voice from weeping,' 31:16, and 'set up the roadmarks,' 31:21, are invitations to hope and to prepare for the return, not rules for later generations.

The passage shows a pattern worth carrying forward, which is that God's discipline and God's love are not opposites. The line 'I will discipline you justly,' 30:11, sits beside 'I have loved you with an everlasting love,' 31:3. The reader who has been disciplined is not told to doubt love, and the one who is comfortable is not told to forget discipline. Applying the new covenant is also a matter of care. The New Testament says that believers in Christ now share in it, Hebrews 8:6 and 10:15 to 18, but it also says that Israel's own promise has not been cancelled, Romans 11:26 to 29, and that the full gathering and the rebuilt city still lie ahead. The text should not be treated as a vague blessing for everyone nor as a promise that has nothing to do with the church.

debates.question: What is the new covenant, and who are 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah'?

views.label: Fulfilled in the church through Christ
views.case: The New Testament quotes the promise as fulfilled in Jesus' blood, Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:6 to 13, and Paul's ministers of the new covenant, 2 Corinthians 3:6, are Jews and Gentiles together. On this view the church, as the people of the new covenant, is the Israel of the promise, and Hebrews says the first covenant is obsolete, 8:13.

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ and still to be completed for national Israel
views.case: Others argue that the New Testament's use shows the covenant inaugurated at the cross, and that Romans 11:26 to 29, which quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah's covenant language, shows that Israel as a people will be gathered. The promises of land and city in 31:38 to 40 and 32:37 to 41 are then to be fulfilled as well. The new covenant is one covenant with a present and a future stage.

views.label: Fulfilled in the new creation as a whole
views.case: A third reading says that the covenant's promises, including the law written on every heart and the end of the need to say 'Know the LORD,' find their consummation only when God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The present church has the first fruits, 2 Corinthians 1:22, and the final knowing awaits.

debates.bearing: All three confess that Christ's blood is the covenant's basis and that the Spirit is already writing the law on hearts. They differ on the shape of the future.

debates.question: What does 'a woman will shelter a man' mean in 31:22?

views.label: Israel will seek the LORD
views.case: Israel is called a 'virgin' and a 'daughter' in these chapters, so the woman is the nation and the man is the LORD, whom she will encircle with her devotion. The new thing is a reversal of her faithlessness: she who wandered will now turn and cling to Him. The BSB footnote offers 'surround' and 'return to' as alternatives.

views.label: A reversal of ordinary roles
views.case: Others see a proverbial statement of a world turned upside down, in which a woman takes the protective role of a warrior, a sign of how complete and safe the restoration will be, with no need for armed men. This view stays with the context of security in 31:23 to 25.

views.label: A hint of the Messiah's birth
views.case: Many church fathers and later interpreters heard it as a pointer to the woman who would carry the child who is Lord, Mary and Jesus. This reading finds support in the phrase 'a new thing,' but it is a later reading, and few commentators claim the verse's first meaning was a prophecy of the virgin birth.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is hard, and a safe conclusion is that the verse promises something startling and new. It is wise to hold any reading with humility.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice is the repetition of shuv, the verb of turning and returning. In 31:18 Ephraim prays, 'Restore me, that I may return,' where the Hebrew puts the causative and the plain stem of the same verb side by side: turn me, and I will turn. The prayer admits that repentance is God's gift as well as the people's act. In 31:22 the 'faithless daughter' is literally the 'turning' or 'backsliding' daughter, and the question 'how long will you wander?' plays on the same root. A verb that began as a charge against Israel, 3:12 and 3:22, is now a promise.

In 31:3 the 'loving devotion' is chesed, covenant loyalty, and the verb that goes with it, 'drawn,' means to pull or draw along, as one draws a person out of danger. God's loyalty is not passive. It acts to pull Israel from the place where it was lost.

In 31:20 the heart of God speaks in two phrases. 'My heart yearns for him' is, in the footnote's literal rendering, 'My bowels yearn for him,' the language of the inner parts moved with feeling, and 'I have great compassion' is the verb racham in a doubled form, 'I will surely have compassion,' from the same root that gives the word for the womb. The picture is of a parent. Hosea 11:8 has the same emotion. The sentence just before has God saying, 'I still remember him,' where the Hebrew puts 'remember, I will remember' with the sense of still. In 31:34 the same pair of words returns with a negative: 'I will remember their sins no more.' God remembers Ephraim and does not remember the sin.

In 31:15 Rachel 'refuses to be comforted,' using a form of the verb nacham, which means both to console and to relent. In 31:19 the same root is used for Ephraim's own repentance, 'I repented,' and in 31:13 for God's comfort. The verb carries the whole drama of grief, regret and consolation.

In 31:33 the law is placed 'in their minds,' and the Hebrew is more literally 'within them,' in their inward parts. 'Inscribe on their hearts' uses the verb for writing that the covenant had used for the tablets, Exodus 31:18. In 31:32 the covenant they broke is a covenant in which God says 'I was a husband to them.' The footnote notes that the Greek reads 'I disregarded them,' and Hebrews 8:9 follows the Greek. The two readings need not conflict: the husband who was spurned also set them aside in discipline.

In 30:12 the wound is 'incurable,' a word used of Jeremiah's own pain in 15:18, and the promise of healing in 30:17 answers his question in 8:22, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' The oath in 31:35 to 36 speaks of the 'fixed order' of sun, moon and stars, a word for decrees, and then says Israel will cease to be a nation only if those decrees cease. The covenant with Israel is bound with the covenant of creation.

Finally, in 31:28 God says that as He 'watched over' them to uproot, so He will watch to build. The verb is the one of the almond branch in 1:11 to 12, and the list of six verbs is that of Jeremiah's call, 1:10. The prophet who was appointed to uproot and to build now sees the second half done.

typology.type: The Davidic king raised up, 30:9 and 30:21
typology.fulfillment: God promises that Israel will serve 'David their king, whom I will raise up for them,' and that their leader will arise from among them and be brought near to God. This sits with the Branch of Jeremiah 23:5 to 6 and the shepherd of Ezekiel 34:23. In Christ the correspondence is exact: the angel says that God will give Him the throne of His father David, Luke 1:32, and Hebrews says He draws near as a priest, Hebrews 7:25. The question 'who would dare to approach?' is answered by the one who brings us near, Ephesians 2:18. The type falls short in that the earthly kings failed to bring the people to God.

typology.type: Rachel's weeping and the children who return
typology.fulfillment: Rachel weeps at Ramah for children who 'are no more,' and God answers that they will return from the enemy's land, 31:15 to 17. Matthew sees the same grief in the slaughter of the infants at Bethlehem, Matthew 2:17 to 18, and the child who escaped is the one through whom the exile ends. Jesus says that the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and live, John 5:25, and Paul says that the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26. The type falls short because the return from the land of the enemy in Jeremiah's day was not a return from death.

typology.type: The new covenant and the rebuilt city
typology.fulfillment: The covenant written on the heart and the city that will 'never again be uprooted,' 31:31 to 40, are paired in the oracle. Hebrews sets them side by side, saying that believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem and to Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 12:22 to 24. John sees the city come down, Revelation 21:2. The escalation is that the city no longer needs a temple. The type falls short in that the rebuilt Jerusalem after the exile was again destroyed.

The wound that no physician could treat, 30:12 to 13, is healed by God, 30:17. Peter says of Christ that 'by His wounds you were healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, drawing on Isaiah 53:5, and the healed are those who were straying like sheep. The escalation is that the cure comes through the Healer's own wounding. The type falls short in that the wound of Judah was national, while the healing of the cross reaches the root of sin.

study.christ:
The most direct line from this passage to Christ is the one He drew Himself. On the night He was betrayed, after supper, He took the cup and said, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you,' Luke 22:20. He said it in a room where the disciples knew the prophets, and they would have heard the phrase 'new covenant' only in one place, Jeremiah 31:31. Hebrews, quoting the whole promise, makes the claim explicit: Jesus has received a more excellent ministry, 'founded on better promises,' Hebrews 8:6, and in His death the promise of forgiveness is fulfilled, so that 'an offering for sin is no longer needed,' Hebrews 10:18.

Each part of the covenant finds its centre in Him. The law written within is the work of His Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:3 and Romans 8:3 to 4, and the knowledge of God 'from the least to the greatest' is what Jesus gives: 'No one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him,' Matthew 11:27. John 6:45 quotes Isaiah on being taught by God and applies it to those who come to Jesus. The final promise, 'I will forgive their iniquities and remember their sins no more,' rests on the sacrifice that Hebrews 10 says was offered once for all.

The Davidic promise of 30:9 and 30:21 is realised in the King who is also the priest who draws near. The shepherd who gathers, 31:10, is the one who says, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11. The love that drew Israel is the love that God showed 'in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. Rachel's weeping is answered by the Child who survived Herod to bring the great reversal.

The chapter also sets the shape of Christian experience. The prayer 'Restore me, that I may return,' 31:18, is the prayer that grace answers. The believer's turning is itself a gift of the one who turns the heart.

A caution is in order. The chapter's first meaning is God's promise to the exiles of Israel and Judah, and its larger fulfilment should not erase that. And not every detail is a picture of Jesus: the tambourines of 31:4 and the vineyards of 31:5 are not coded messages. The links rest on the New Testament's own citations, and they are strong.
study.god:
The first thing to say is that God is the speaker of every promise here, and He says 'I' on nearly every line: I will restore, I will break, I will heal, I will build, I will make, I will write, I will forgive. The restoration is entirely His work. He gives no job to the exiles other than to turn and receive it.

He is the God of love that is older than the sin. 'I have loved you with an everlasting love,' 31:3, says that His love did not begin with Israel's good behaviour and so cannot end with its bad. The same God says, 'I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished,' 30:11, and 'because of your great iniquity,' 30:15. The two are held together. His discipline is real, and it is never the full account of His heart: 'Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me?' 31:20.

He is a God of feeling. 'My heart yearns for him' puts into His mouth the language of a parent whose child has gone away. It is not the language of an impassive deity. The God who reasons and rules in this book is also the one who is moved to the depths, and Scripture does not treat the two as contradictory.

He is the God of the new thing. 'The LORD has created a new thing in the land,' 31:22, and 'a new covenant,' 31:31, say that He is not bound to repeat the past. He can do what the old order could not, and He does it by changing the people from the inside.

He is also the God of fixed order. The oath of 31:35 to 37 sets His faithfulness beside the sun and the moon, and the sea, and gives a sign as sure as creation itself. Because He is the Creator, His promise cannot be less stable than the heavens.

For worship, the chapter calls us to sing, as it says, 'Sing with joy for Jacob,' 31:7, and to pray the prayer of 31:18. It teaches us to receive forgiveness as full and final, and to accept both the discipline and the love of the God who does both.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah's call lists six verbs: to uproot and tear down, destroy and overthrow, build and plant. Jeremiah 31:28 picks up the same verbs and says that God will now watch over the building and planting. The consolation is the second half of the prophet's call.

Jeremiah asked whether there was no balm in Gilead and why the health of his people was not restored. Jeremiah 30:17 is God's answer: I will restore your health and heal your wounds. The prophet's grief meets its reply.

A new heart and a new spirit, with God's Spirit within His people. It sets out how the law will come to be written on the heart in Jeremiah 31:33, and shows that the new covenant works by the gift of the Spirit.

Ezekiel answers the same proverb about sour grapes and teaches that each person is responsible before God. It is a close companion to Jeremiah 31:29 to 30, and it shows that both prophets were addressing the same exiles' complaint.

God asks how He could give Ephraim up, and says that His heart is turned within Him. It is the nearest parallel to Jeremiah 31:20, where God's inner being yearns for Ephraim, and it shows the depth of feeling behind the promise.

The evangelist hears the exile's grief again in Herod's cruelty at Bethlehem. Jeremiah's next verses, which promise that the children will come back from the enemy's land, shadow the child who escaped and the greater return He brings.

Jesus names the cup the new covenant in His blood. It is the one place in the Gospels where He uses Jeremiah's phrase, and it declares that the promise of Jeremiah 31:31 is now being kept at the table of the Last Supper.
A long quotation. It gives the whole of Jeremiah 31:31 to 34 in the middle of the letter and argues that Christ mediates a better covenant on better promises, and that the first has become obsolete.

Quotes the central promises again, the law on hearts and sins remembered no more, and draws the conclusion that where forgiveness is complete there is no more offering for sin. It shows how the forgiveness of Jeremiah 31:34 works.
Paul contrasts ink and stone with the Spirit and the human heart, and calls himself a minister of a new covenant. It shows the inward writing of Jeremiah 31:33 at work in a living congregation.

Paul quotes the promise to take away sin and says that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. It ties the new covenant to the future of Israel and answers the oath of Jeremiah 31:36 that Israel will not cease to be a nation.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is a story of covenants, and Jeremiah 30 and 31 are where the Old Testament's account of failed covenants turns toward a final one. God made covenant with Noah, Genesis 9:9 to 11, with Abraham, Genesis 15:18, with Israel at Sinai, Exodus 24:7 to 8, and with David, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16. Each was real, and each, in the history of the people, was broken or strained by human failure. By Jeremiah's day the nation that had been brought out of Egypt 'by the hand' had broken the covenant, 31:32, and the covenant curses had fallen.

Jeremiah's block of consolation answers the question that the whole history raises: if the people cannot keep the covenant, how can God's purpose succeed? The answer is that He will do what the people cannot, by writing His law within them and by forgiving their sins. That is the same answer that the story of Genesis had begun to give. The curse of Genesis 3 had left a people with a heart turned from God. The promise of a seed, Genesis 3:15, awaits the day when the heart is changed.

The passage looks forward in at least three ways. It points to the cross, where the covenant is sealed in blood, Luke 22:20. It points to Pentecost and the gift of the Spirit, Acts 2:17 and Ezekiel 36:27, where the law begins to be written inwardly. And it points to the end, where 'they will all know Me' reaches its fullness, and the dwelling of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The tears that Rachel could not stop are wiped away, Revelation 21:4, the 'incurable wound' is healed, and the city that is never again uprooted comes down from God.

Until that day, the church lives under the new covenant and awaits its completion. It knows God, it is forgiven, and it has the Spirit, and yet it still prays 'Restore me, that I may return,' and still waits for the gathering of all God's people. The Book of Consolation tells the church that the God who began the work will finish it, Philippians 1:6, and that the promise is as sure as the fixed order of the sun and the moon.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle - Part 4
sermon.why: Carson preaches directly through Jeremiah 30-31, tracing the movement from the day of Jacob's trouble to the new covenant promise, and shows how the whole Book of Consolation finds its fulfillment in Christ.

quiz.q: What is the day of Jacob's trouble in Jeremiah 30:7, and what is its ultimate outcome?

options.text: A time of unmatched distress for God's people, out of which He promises they will be saved.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly pairs the severity of the distress with the promise that Jacob will be saved out of it.

options.text: A day of final, total destruction with no promise of survival.
options.note: The verse explicitly promises that Jacob will be saved out of this distress, not destroyed by it.

options.text: A minor, brief inconvenience for the exiles.
options.note: The text describes it as unmatched distress, none will be like it, not something minor.

options.text: A day that only affects the surrounding nations, not Israel.
options.note: The distress is specifically named as Jacob's own trouble, though surrounding nations are addressed elsewhere in the passage.

quiz.q: What does God promise regarding Rachel's weeping in Jeremiah 31:15-17?

options.text: That her weeping will be answered with hope, for her children will return from the land of the enemy.
options.note: Verses 16 to 17 directly answer the weeping of verse 15 with the promise of the children's return.

options.text: That the weeping is final and will never be comforted.
options.note: The text explicitly commands, keep your voice from weeping, because comfort and return are promised.

options.text: That Rachel herself would be resurrected immediately.
options.note: The promise concerns the return of her children, the exiled people, not a literal resurrection of Rachel.

options.text: That the weeping refers only to a single, unrelated historical event with no future promise attached.
options.note: The weeping is directly tied to the specific promise of hope and return in the same passage.

quiz.q: According to Jeremiah 31:31-34, what makes the new covenant different from the covenant made at the exodus?

options.text: God will put His law within His people and write it on their hearts, and He will forgive their sins completely, remembering them no more.
options.note: Verses 33 to 34 name both the internal transformation and the complete forgiveness as the new covenant's distinguishing marks.

options.text: It requires stricter external rules than the covenant made at Sinai.
options.note: The new covenant is marked by internal transformation, not additional external rules.

options.text: It is made only with a small remnant and excludes the rest of Israel and Judah.
options.note: The text explicitly names both the house of Israel and the house of Judah as recipients.

options.text: It is identical in every respect to the covenant made at the exodus.
options.note: Verse 32 explicitly contrasts it with that covenant, which Israel broke; it is not identical.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament identify the fulfillment of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31?

options.text: Jesus names the cup at the Last Supper the new covenant in His blood, and Hebrews quotes the passage to show it fulfilled in Christ's priesthood and sacrifice.
options.note: Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:8-12 both directly connect this promise to Christ's own words and work.

options.text: The New Testament never references this promise.
options.note: Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:8-12 both directly quote or invoke this exact passage.

options.text: It is fulfilled only in a future political kingdom with no connection to Christ's death.
options.note: The New Testament ties the new covenant directly to Christ's blood and sacrifice, not merely a future political arrangement.

options.text: It is treated as a minor, symbolic reference with no bearing on the sacraments.
options.note: Jesus applies this promise directly to the cup of the Last Supper, giving it central sacramental significance.

quiz.q: What guarantees the certainty of God's covenant faithfulness in Jeremiah 31:35-37?

options.text: It is compared to the fixed order of the sun, moon, stars, and sea, as unbreakable as creation itself.
options.note: Verses 35 to 37 explicitly ground God's covenant faithfulness in the fixed, unchangeable order of creation.

options.text: It depends entirely on Israel's own future faithfulness.
options.note: The passage grounds the promise in God's fixed created order, not in Israel's own performance.

options.text: It is left uncertain and conditional throughout the passage.
options.note: The passage presents the promise as certain, comparing it to the fixed order of creation, not as uncertain.

options.text: It is guaranteed by the continued existence of the Babylonian empire.
options.note: The guarantee comes from God's own created order, not from any human empire's continuation.

questions: Jacob's distress was real and severe, yet God promised he would be saved out of it, not spared from it entirely. Where are you needing to trust that God will bring you through hardship rather than simply remove it?
God says of Zion, they call you an outcast, for whom no one cares, but I will restore your health. Where do you feel like an outcast, and how does it change things to know God cares even there?
The new covenant promises God's law written on the heart, not merely known in the mind. Where is there a gap between what you know is true and what actually governs your heart and affections?
Under the new covenant, sins are forgiven and remembered no more. Is there a sin you have confessed but still cannot believe God has truly forgotten?
God's faithfulness is compared to the fixed order of sun, moon, and sea. Where do you need that same steady confidence in God's promises this week?

translationNotes.note: The time of Jacob's distress became a phrase later applied in Jewish and Christian interpretation to a final period of tribulation before decisive deliverance, though in its immediate context it refers first to the distress of exile itself.

Ramah was near the traditional site of Rachel's tomb and a gathering point for exiles being marched to Babylon, giving the image of Rachel weeping for her children a vivid, geographically specific setting.

This verse contains the only occurrence of the phrase new covenant in the entire Old Testament, and it is quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8-12, making it one of the most directly quoted Old Testament passages in the New Testament.
